title: Moisture sources and building history
audience: Supervisors, coordinators and trained cleaners who may be asked to triage, refer or document mould-related work in homes, rentals and commercial buildings, under an approved plan. Not a qualification or authority to remediate, demolish, or certify any building or room.
learningOutcomes: Complete a non-invasive moisture-history questionnaire for a fictional property.
Separate observed, reported and assumed information in a photograph log.
Refer the question of the moisture source to a qualified building investigation.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers history-taking and referral. It does not authorise opening walls, roofs, subfloors or cavities to find the source. A qualified building investigation does that work under an approved plan.

instruction.heading: Mould follows moisture
instruction.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says the source of moisture must be located so that the cause is addressed and recurrence is prevented. It lists common sources as water accumulation, condensation, poor ventilation, severe weather and occupant behaviour. It also says mould is likely if building foundations or porous components stay wet for more than 48 hours. The same guideline's flood appendix says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes, so the time since a water event matters. Find out when the water came in, not only where the stain is.

instruction.heading: Building history and the photograph log
instruction.body: Use a non-invasive moisture-history questionnaire. Ask when the stain first appeared, what happens during rain, showers, cooking and drying, whether the roof, gutters or plumbing have been repaired, and what the occupants have done about it. Keep a photograph log with the date and the location of each photograph, and note who reported each fact. Keep observation and assumption apart. A newly painted wall that smells musty after rain, while the carpet next to it feels dry, shows that the source may be somewhere other than where it seems. Refer the question of source to a qualified building investigation.

instruction.heading: Why the source must be corrected first
instruction.body: Cleaning or repainting a source that is still wet will not stop the growth. The guideline says surfaces should not be painted, sealed or covered until they are dry, and it treats repair of the source as a core part of remediation. Map the order of the work: source identified and repaired, moisture re-evaluated, drying complete, and only then cleaning and finishing.

procedure: Interview the occupant or owner using the non-invasive questionnaire.
Record the dates of any water event, leak, flood or repair.
Photograph the affected areas from outside any cavity, with dates and locations.
Separate what was observed from what was reported and what is assumed.
Refer the question of source to a qualified building investigation.
Make no cleaning or repainting decision that depends on a source that has not been identified.

workedExamples.situation: A newly painted wall smells musty after rain, and the carpet next to it feels dry.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct next step?
workedExamples.reasoning: The source has not been identified and may be somewhere other than the visible area. Record the observations, use the questionnaire and photograph log, and refer the source to a qualified building investigation. Repainting would not correct the source, and the guideline says not to paint until surfaces are dry.

workedExamples.situation: The owner says a leak was fixed last winter, but the stain has returned this month.
workedExamples.reasoning: The earlier repair may not have fixed the source, or water may be entering elsewhere. Record the dates, the repair history and the return of the stain, and refer for re-evaluation before any cleaning plan is set.

equipmentAndPpe: Moisture-history questionnaire, printed or on a tablet.
Photograph log with a date, location and reporter for each entry.
Training-only fictional property file. No real building is inspected in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Painting or cleaning over a damp area and calling it fixed.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify and correct the moisture source first, then re-evaluate.

commonErrors.error: Treating the first visible leak as the only possible source.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask the history questions and refer for a qualified investigation.

commonErrors.error: Drawing conclusions from one visit without the history.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the questionnaire, the photograph log and the dates together.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Opening cavities or disturbing building materials to find the source is outside this lesson and needs a competent, authorised person.
The 48-hour and 24 to 48-hour timings are statements in the WA Department of Health guideline. They are not national rules.

qualityStandard: The learner completes the questionnaire and photograph log for a fictional property.
The learner separates observation, report and assumption in the record.
The learner refers the source question without opening any cavity.
documentationEvidence: Photograph log with dates, locations and reporters.
Referral note to the qualified building investigation.
summary: Mould follows moisture, so the source must be found.
History and dates come before any cleaning decision.
Do not paint, seal or cover wet surfaces.
Refer the source, and do not open cavities.

knowledgeChecks.question: A newly painted wall smells musty after rain, and the adjacent carpet is dry. What is the correct next step?
options: Repaint the wall with a stronger paint.
Cut into the wall to see what is behind it.
Record the observations, use the questionnaire and refer the source to a qualified investigation.

knowledgeChecks.question: According to the WA guideline, when should surfaces be painted or sealed?
options: As soon as the leak is found.
Before any drying has started, to keep moisture out.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which list matches the common moisture sources named in the WA guideline?
options: Gas leaks, electrical faults and smoke.
Water accumulation, condensation, poor ventilation, severe weather and occupant behaviour.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.
